Shwedagon wears a queen's weight in gold. The Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon, Myanmar, rises 99 meters. Legend calls it over 2,600 years old, though scholars date it later. Real gold plates and gold leaf cover the whole pagoda. In the 15th century Queen Shin Sawbu gave her weight in gold. That was about 40 kilograms, beaten into gold leaf. At the top sits the hti, an iron umbrella set with jewels. King Mindon donated the current hti in 1871. It is set with more than 4,000 diamonds and many other gems. A diamond of about 76 carats sits at the very top.

Elizabeth I's bracelet held a clock. A Tudor ledger lists an armlet with a clock in its clasp. The Earl of Leicester gave it to her for New Year. The armlet is lost, and its famous picture is a 1926 ad. In 1810 the Queen of Naples ordered a bracelet watch from Breguet. Breguet finished it in 1812 on a woven hair and gold strap. In 1868 Patek Philippe made a bracelet watch for a Hungarian countess. A lid set with rose cut diamonds covered the watch. By 1887 papers called gold bracelet watches a pretty and useful ornament. Most men held out until the First World War.

#wristwatch #watchhistory #breguet #patekphilippe #jewelryhistory

The Armada Jewel postdates the Armada. It is a gold locket made around 1600, and its Armada name is a later popular title. The front shows Elizabeth I in gold, under rock crystal. It is set with diamonds and rubies. A miniature of the queen inside was painted by Nicholas Hilliard. The back shows the English Church as an ark on stormy seas, and its Latin motto speaks of calm through fierce waves. Tradition says Elizabeth I gave it to Sir Thomas Heneage. The V&A says there is no evidence for that story. It reached the V&A in 1935 after a Christie's auction.

#armadajewel #elizabethi #tudorjewelry #hilliard #jewelryhistory

A Silla crown dangles 58 jade commas. Silla was a Korean kingdom, and its royal tombs held gold crowns. One found in 1921 gave its tomb the name Gold Crown. A gold band carries three tree shapes and two antler shapes. One theory calls the trees a world tree joining heaven and earth. Gold rivets fasten the branches to the band. Small gold discs called spangles hang from it on gold wire. Curved jade beads called gogok hang there too. One crown, from the Heavenly Horse Tomb, carries 58 of them. That crown stands 32.5 centimeters tall.

#silla #koreanhistory #goldcrown #gyeongju #jewelryhistory

Two Nobel medals once hid in acid. Germany had just occupied Denmark in April 1940. Chemist Georg de Hevesy worked at Niels Bohr's institute in Copenhagen, and he dissolved two German laureates' medals in strong acid. The flask sat on a shelf and the Nazis never noticed. After the war the gold was recovered and new medals were made. Franck's new medal was presented in Chicago in 1952. Today the medals are 18 karat gold with a 24 karat gold coat. Most are 66 millimeters across and weigh about 175 grams. Erik Lindberg designed four of the medals. The Peace medal was designed by sculptor Gustav Vigeland.

All mined gold fits in one cube. By the end of 2025 about 220,000 tonnes had been mined, and gold is so dense that the pile is smaller than you think. The cube would be roughly 22 meters on each side. It would fill about four and a half Olympic pools. About 45 percent of it is jewelry. Mines add more than 3,000 tonnes a year. Estimates for gold still underground run from 55,000 to 66,000 tonnes. A gold treasure from Varna, Bulgaria is over 6,000 years old. That treasure holds about 3,000 gold objects.

#gold #goldmining #worldgoldcouncil #goldfacts #jewelryhistory

Eggs can quickly blacken silver. Tarnish is silver sulfide, made when silver meets sulfur, and sulfur gas in the air is the main cause of tarnish. Eggs and wool both give off sulfur. Thin layers look yellow or blue before turning black, and a thicker layer actually slows further tarnishing. Sterling tarnishes faster because its copper reacts too. Foil in hot baking soda water forms a tiny battery, and the sulfur moves from the silver to the aluminum. Museums wrap silver in cloth that traps sulfur. Silver in regular use stays bright longer.

#silvertarnish #silverjewelry #sterlingsilver #jewelrycare #jewelryhistory

Baroque probably began as a pearl word. A baroque pearl is noticeably irregular, with no apparent symmetry. Dictionaries say it likely comes from Portuguese barroco, an irregular pearl, and only later did the word name an art style. Around 1600 goldsmiths used lumpy pearls as the bodies of creatures. In a Met pendant, one pearl is a sea monster's body. Another pendant uses a pearl for the torso of a centaur. A Cheapside Hoard pin has a pearl for a ship's hull. Its mast and rigging are made of gold wire. The hoard was unearthed in London in 1912.

#baroque #baroquepearl #pearls #renaissancejewelry #jewelryhistory

Celluloid plastic could pass for ivory. It is often called the first commercially successful plastic. It was made from nitrocellulose softened with camphor. It is credited to John Wesley Hyatt, a printer by trade. It copied costly materials like ivory and coral. By the 1880s, fake tortoiseshell combs were selling well. Ivory look pieces were often sold as French Ivory. In 1878, Hyatt got a US patent for making combs from celluloid. It made look alikes of fine goods affordable to many. In the 1920s, DuPont sold celluloid dresser sets as Pyralin. Around 1900, celluloid also gave ping pong balls their bounce.

#celluloid #vintagejewelry #plastic #antiquejewelry #jewelryhistory

Unplated white gold is faintly yellow. White gold is gold mixed with white metals such as palladium, and an 18 karat piece is 75 percent gold. So jewelers plate it with rhodium for a bright white shine. Rhodium is a silvery white metal related to platinum. William Hyde Wollaston found it in the early 1800s, and its name is Greek for rose, after the color of its salts. The plating is often about a micron thick. It wears off, so rings are often re-plated every year or two. Platinum is usually left unplated because it is naturally white. In 2021 only about 24 tonnes of rhodium were mined.

#whitegold #rhodium #rhodiumplating #jewelrycare #jewelryhistory

Girandole earrings share a name with fireworks. It comes from Italian girandola, tied to a verb meaning to turn. In English it first meant a firework in the 1600s. The same word also names a branched candlestick. The earrings are named after that candlestick. The classic design is a bow with three pear shaped drops. They were a leading earring style of the 1700s. Some were made in glass paste instead of gems. Heavy pairs could be tied to the hair with a ribbon. When the style faded, many pairs were taken apart and reused. A Paris pattern book from 1770 showed girandole designs.

#girandole #earrings #georgianjewelry #antiquejewelry #jewelryhistory

The safety pin began as jewelry. Ancient brooch pins called fibulae are over 3,000 years old. One end is a spring and the other hooks into a catch. Some early ones are shaped like a violin bow, and Roman crossbow brooches were a status symbol. The word fibula is Latin for clasp or pin. It comes from a verb meaning to fasten. In 1849 Walter Hunt of New York patented a dress pin, made from a single piece of wire. MIT's Lemelson Center says Hunt improved an ancient Roman jewelry idea. His patent is United States number 6,281.

#safetypin #fibula #ancientjewelry #brooch #jewelryhistory

Jewel likely began as a Latin joke. Most dictionaries trace it to jocus, the Latin word for game. It reached English from French, as jouel, around the year 1300. Gem comes from the Latin word for a bud. Americans write jewelry, and the British write jewellery. In a watch, a jewel is a tiny ruby or sapphire bearing. A hard jewel keeps a pivot hole from wearing out of shape. An English patent from 1704 covered piercing rubies for watches. A typical mechanical watch has about 17 jewels. Bijou probably comes from a Breton word for finger ring.

#jewel #wordorigins #etymology #watchjewels #jewelryhistory

This tiara was a wedding gift twice. The Girls of Great Britain and Ireland gave it in 1893. The bride was Mary of Teck, who married on July 6. Lady Greville led the committee, and it bought the tiara from Garrard. Leftover money, at Mary's request, went to HMS Victoria widows and orphans. Diamond festoons and scrolls were once topped with large pearls, and in 1914, Mary swapped the pearls for diamonds. In 1947, now Queen Mary, she gave it to her granddaughter Elizabeth. It was a wedding present, and Elizabeth's first tiara. It is reportedly nicknamed Granny's Tiara, and Elizabeth II is shown wearing it on banknotes and coins.

Moss agate contains no moss at all. In many stones, manganese or iron oxides form the shapes. Dendrite comes from the Greek word for tree. Mineral water seeping through cracks grows those branching shapes. They can look so like plants that they pass for fossils. It lacks the banding of true agate, but the name stuck. Cutters shape it into smooth domes called cabochons. It is about 6.5 to 7 on the Mohs scale, like quartz. Mocha stone, its old name, points to a Red Sea port. That same port gave coffee the word mocha.

#mossagate #agate #dendrites #gemstones #jewelryhistory

Ground malachite painted Egyptian eyelids green. Egyptians used it as eye paint roughly 6,000 years ago. The name comes from the Greek word for mallow, a green plant. It forms above copper deposits, so it guided prospectors. Its bands record changing water as the stone grew. The most prized pattern is rounded rings like eyes. It is soft, about 3.5 to 4 on the Mohs scale. Big Russian malachite pieces were veneers of thin matched sheets. Saint Isaac's Cathedral in Saint Petersburg has ten malachite columns. Scientists tested Gutenberg Bibles with a laser and found malachite green.

#malachite #ancientegypt #gemstones #greenstone #jewelryhistory

This gem has two different hardnesses. It is kyanite, named from the Greek word for blue. Along its long axis, hardness is about 4 to 4.5, and across that axis, it is about 6 to 7. Sources vary a little, so treat those numbers as close estimates. Its old name, disthene, means double strength in Greek. It is mostly blue, but also comes in green and orange, and orange kyanite from Tanzania gets its color from manganese. Its perfect cleavage and varied hardness make it hard to cut. Earrings and pendants suit it, while rings need protective settings.

#kyanite #bluegemstone #gemology #gemstones #jewelrylovers

The oldest known beads are snail shells. 33 shells from a Moroccan cave are at least 142,000 years old. Wear marks suggest they were hung on strings or clothing. Researchers suggest beads helped people show identity without words. At Blombos Cave in South Africa, beads are about 75,000 years old. The holes match ones made by pushing a bone point through. In Algeria, a shell bead was found up to 200 kilometers inland. Researchers suggest early beads worked like gifts that built friendships. The same sea snail turns up from Morocco to Israel.

#beads #shellbeads #archaeology #ancientjewelry #jewelryhistory

Fluorescence is named after the mineral fluorite. George Stokes coined the word in 1852, from fluorspar. Its name comes from a Latin word meaning to flow. Metalmakers once used it as a flux. The element fluorine is also named after the mineral. Fluorite is soft, so it suits earrings better than rings. Traces of other elements give it nearly every color. Blue John is a banded purple and blue fluorite from Derbyshire. In Britain it comes only from two caverns near Castleton. In 1768, Matthew Boulton asked for a mine lease to make vases. Raw Blue John is dried about a year, then soaked in resin.

#fluorite #bluejohn #fluorescence #gemstones #jewelryhistory

This diamond sold for over $48 million. It is the Blue Moon of Josephine, at 12.03 carats. GIA graded it Fancy Vivid blue and Internally Flawless, and boron in the diamond is what makes it blue. Its 29.62-carat rough came from South Africa's Cullinan mine in 2014, and Cora International paid about $25.6 million for that rough. Cora then spent months cutting and polishing it. Sotheby's sold it in Geneva in November 2015. With fees, the price was close to $48.5 million, which is over $4 million a carat, an auction record. The buyer renamed it for his daughter Josephine, then seven.

#bluediamond #bluemoonofjosephine #diamonds #sothebys #jewelryhistory

Some stickpins were topped with gold nuggets. A stickpin held the folds of a slippery silk cravat in place. Men were already wearing them in the early 1800s. Victorian men wore very little jewelry, so a stickpin showed taste. Heads ranged from a single pearl to a carved cameo. Playful heads showed little animals and horseshoes. Some heads were real nuggets, or pieces of quartz holding gold. Some pins came in pairs joined by a fine chain. In the 1920s, Cartier made a clicking pin for lapels and hats. Stickpins faded as slimmer ties and tie clips took over.

#stickpin #cravatpin #victorianjewelry #mensjewelry #jewelryhistory

Locket once meant a window bar. It comes from French loquet, meaning a latch or bolt. In the 1300s it meant an iron bar fastening a window. The little hinged case is first recorded in the late 1600s. Lockets grew out of hinged pendants that held holy relics. Elizabeth I's locket ring from about 1575 hides two portraits. The Heneage Jewel is a locket holding a miniature of the queen. By about 1850, daguerreotype portraits sat inside lockets. Soon lockets paired a photograph with a lock of hair. A hinge on one side and a small catch opposite close it.

#locket #etymology #tudorjewelry #victorianjewelry #jewelryhistory

Rose gold was once called Russian gold. It was popular in Russia in the early 1800s, and it has other names too, like pink gold and red gold. Rose gold is gold mixed with copper, and sometimes some silver. 18 karat rose gold is 75 percent pure gold, and copper and a little silver make up the rest. The jeweler Fabergé also worked with rose gold. In the 1920s, it became fashionable in the United States. Most sources call it more durable than yellow gold, karat for karat. Its color runs through the metal, so it is not plated. The more copper in the mix, the redder the gold.

#rosegold #russiangold #goldjewelry #jewelryfacts #fabergé

Niello helped inspire early printmaking. The word comes from Latin nigellum, meaning blackish. It is a black mix of sulfur and metals such as silver. Lines are engraved and filled with niello powder or paste. Heat fuses it in place, then the surface is polished flush. Pliny wrote the earliest known niello recipe in the 1st century AD. A Roman panther brooch has its spots inlaid in niello. Byzantine silver carried niello by the middle of the 6th century. Tula, Russia, grew so famous for niello it was called Tula work. Florentine goldsmith Maso Finiguerra's paper proofs of niello helped inspire printmaking.

#niello #silversmith #byzantine #printmaking #jewelryhistory

Jewelry render details: what an ear wire is

Jewelry rendering, step by step: https://www.heygema.com/en/jewelry-rendering

An ear wire is the wire that passes through the earlobe, and jewelers also call it a fish hook or French hook. Its end is open, so it can slip out when snagged, and a small rubber stopper can help hold it in place. The drop hangs from a small loop in the wire, and heavier drops often use a leverback, whose hinge snaps shut. Many ear wires are about 20 gauge, and nickel-free titanium wires suit people with sensitive ears. The renders in this video were made with HeyGema.

#earwire #earrings #jewelrymaking #jewelryrendering #jewelrydesign

A hand crank cuts guilloché patterns. Guilloché is a pattern cut into metal by a rose engine. The machine rocks the metal against a patterned disc called a rosette. A straight line machine cuts straight lines, like Clous de Paris. Both are cranked by hand while the other hand guides the cutter. The grooves are only 30 to 40 microns deep. Translucent enamel is fused over the cuts, so the pattern shows through. Fabergé used the same trick from the 1880s. Breguet made engine turned watch dials famous from 1786. Workshops still cut dials on machines more than a century old.

#guilloche #roseengine #enamel #watchdials #jewelryhistory

Colored titanium works like a soap bubble. Light reflecting from a clear oxide film makes the colors, and the film is a few hundred nanometers thick at most. Robert Hooke studied these thin film colors in 1665. Anodizing grows the film, and more voltage makes it thicker. Ten to fifteen volts gives a brown or bronze, and the exact colors shift with the chemical bath used. Niobium, a related metal, takes colors the same way. The color cannot peel off, but rubbing can wear it away. Titanium is as strong as steel with much less weight. Titanium jewelry began in Birmingham, England, in the mid 1960s.

#titanium #anodizing #metaljewelry #niobium #jewelrymaking

Green powder turns shakudo black. Shakudo means red copper, an alloy with a few percent gold. Its black color appears only after the surface is treated. Makers simmer it in a hot rokusho solution of copper salts. Rokusho itself is a green blue copper powder. Grated daikon radish is part of the traditional process. The finished color is a deep blue black, sometimes purple. Rows of tiny punched domes, called nanako, give a fish roe texture. It decorated sword fittings such as guards and grip ornaments. After 1876, Meiji makers turned shakudo fittings into small jewelry.

Cast rings use a 6,000-year-old method. It is called lost-wax casting, because the wax model melts away. A jeweler surrounds a wax model with a plaster-like mix, and a kiln burns the wax out, leaving a hollow mold. Burnout can reach about 1,350 degrees Fahrenheit, or 732 Celsius. Molten metal is pulled in by vacuum or centrifugal force. A copper amulet from Mehrgarh, in Pakistan, is about 6,000 years old, and many of the 442 objects in an Israeli hoard were lost-wax cast. Goldsmiths in the ancient Americas also cast gold this way. Many jewelers now cast from 3D-printed patterns instead of hand-carved wax.

Collectors smell Bakelite to test it. Chemist Leo Baekeland made Bakelite in 1907. It is often called the first fully synthetic plastic. Once heat sets it, Bakelite stays hard and never melts again. The patent was filed in 1907 and granted in 1909. Makers began using it for costume jewelry in the 1920s. It boomed in the 1930s, when carved bangles were an affordable luxury. Collectors prize rare colors such as cobalt blue. Catalin is Bakelite's cast cousin, known for brighter colors. Hot water or a good rub brings out its chemical smell.

This famous pearl is just two brushstrokes. Johannes Vermeer painted Girl with a Pearl Earring around 1665. A bright dab sits above a soft glow that reflects her collar, and the earring has no visible hook to hold it to her ear. Experts say a real pearl this size would be astronomically expensive. Some think glass, and a 2014 theory says polished tin, but the museum's director says it is neither pearl nor glass, simply paint. Its blue headscarf is natural ultramarine, made from lapis lazuli, and in the 1600s ultramarine was reportedly worth more than gold. Before about 1995, the painting was called Girl with a Turban.

Millefiori glass sometimes hides tiny faces. Millefiori is Italian for a thousand flowers. Makers bundle colored glass rods and stretch them into a long bar. The bar is cut across, and every slice shows the same flower. Slices laid in a disc are heated until they melt together. Alexandria was a leading center for this glass over 2,000 years ago. Venice used it by the 1400s and revived it in the 1800s. Murano makers put tiny portraits inside canes, so slices show faces. One slice from the 1840s shows a man in uniform. Millefiori paperweights became a craze in the mid 1840s.

A Roman cup glows red when backlit. The Lycurgus Cup is a Roman glass cup from the 4th century. Lit from the front, it looks opaque green. Shine light through from behind and the glass glows red. Tiny gold and silver specks in the glass cause the change. The specks are around 50 to 100 nanometers across. That is over 1,000 times smaller than a grain of table salt. Most experts think its figures were cut from a thick glass blank. The figures show King Lycurgus caught in grapevine tendrils. The British Museum bought it from the Rothschild family in 1958.

This jewelry house began with a wedding. In 1895 in Paris, Estelle Arpels married Alfred Van Cleef. Alfred's father cut stones, and Estelle's father dealt in precious stones. Boucheron was the first jeweler on Place Vendôme, in 1893, and its own first boutique opened there in 1906, at number 22. Estelle's brothers later joined to help run the house. At the 1925 Paris Exposition, the house won a Grand Prix, and in 1933 it patented its Mystery Setting. Its ballerina and fairy clips date from 1941. In 1968, it launched Alhambra, a long necklace of four-leaf clovers.

Pietra dura is Italian for hard stones. It is a Florentine art of joining thin slices of colored stone. Each slice is cut to shape and joined edge to edge. The joins are filed so smooth that the seams barely show. Craftsmen used stones such as lapis lazuli and jasper. Rome revived stone inlay in the 1500s, and Florence became a rival. In 1588 Grand Duke Ferdinando de' Medici founded the workshop. It started inside the Uffizi as the Galleria dei Lavori. Florentine pietra dura brooches were popular tourist souvenirs. Today the Opificio delle Pietre Dure restores art in Florence.

Warriors once decorated shields with red coral. The Witham Shield, from Iron Age Britain, has Mediterranean coral, and the Roman writer Pliny said Gauls decorated swords with it too. Red coral is the hard skeleton of tiny sea animals called polyps, and scientists only accepted coral as an animal in the 1700s. A branch thickens by only a fraction of a millimeter a year, and colonies can live for about a century. Licensed scuba divers harvest it 50 meters down or deeper. The red comes from organic pigments in the skeleton. Coral rattles were once teething toys and charms for babies. Torre del Greco in Italy has worked coral for over two centuries.

West Point ring gold flew to space. The class of 1835 got the first West Point class rings. They were signets, cut in reverse to seal letters in wax. Each ring since 1917 has a class crest and a school crest. At graduation it is turned so the school crest faces the heart. Graduates donate old gold rings to be melted into one ingot. A small part, Legacy Gold, is saved for the next melt. So every ring since the class of 2002 holds older gold. In 2025 a locket of Legacy Gold flew to the space station. It flew with an astronaut from that class of 2002.

Oregon sunstone's colors come from copper specks. Smaller specks make it look red, and slightly larger ones green, and one stone can hold up to three colors at once. A 1985 study found metallic copper inside the stones, and Oregon sunstone is sold as natural and untreated. Native Americans may have been the first to collect them, and the first written report came around 1908. Since 1972 the public can collect sunstones free on four square miles. Locals have called them Plush diamonds, and one rough stone from the Dust Devil mine weighed 1,093 carats. Oregon made it the state gemstone in 1987.

Romans wore their keys as rings. A thin hoop held a tiny key set at right angles, and the keys really worked on locks for small boxes. They opened small caskets that held jewelry and other valuables. Roman clothes often lacked pockets, so a ring kept the key close, and a worn key was harder to lose or to steal. Most surviving ones are bronze or iron. Some are only about 2 centimeters across. Museums date them from the 1st to the 4th century AD. Harvard Art Museums and the Met both hold examples.

Black carbonado diamonds once tipped rock drills. Carbonado is a porous black clump of tiny diamond crystals. It is found only in Brazil and the Central African Republic, and long ago South America and Africa were joined. Some studies say it is about 3.8 billion years old. Scientists still debate how it formed, and one 2006 study suggested it may have come from space. Portuguese prospectors named it for its charcoal look. A Brazilian one weighing over 3,000 carats was cut up for drills. A cut carbonado of 555.55 carats sold at Sotheby's in 2022.

This burial suit has 2,498 jade pieces. It belonged to Liu Sheng, who lived in China's Han dynasty, and army engineers found his tomb by chance in 1968. It was the first complete jade suit ever found, and before that suits were known only from old texts. Gold wire weighing about 1,100 grams joins the pieces, and each jade tile has holes at its corners for the wire. Jade was believed to keep a body from decaying. Making one may have taken about ten years. His wife Dou Wan's suit has 2,160 pieces. Liu Sheng's suit is kept at the Hebei Museum in Shijiazhuang.

Meteorite crashes can turn graphite into diamond. Impact diamonds keep the shape of the graphite crystals they replaced. Russia's Popigai crater is about 35.7 million years old and about 100 kilometers across, and geologist Victor Masaitis proved its impact origin in 1971. Russian estimates put its diamonds at over 100 billion carats, but most are tiny and meant for industry, not jewelry. The first diamonds from space were found in 1888. A debated rarer form, lonsdaleite, turned up in a meteorite in 1967. Lonsdaleite is named for Dame Kathleen Lonsdale.

Anglo-Saxon royal garnets traveled thousands of miles. They come from a ship burial at Sutton Hoo in Suffolk, which dates to around 625 and was found in 1939. Its gold shoulder clasps hold garnets and glass. Each garnet is a thin polished plate set in a gold cell, a technique called cloisonné. Beneath each garnet is wafer thin gold foil stamped with a pattern, and the foil bounces light back so the stone glows. In 2023 early scans traced some garnets to India and Sri Lanka. Other garnets were traced to Czechia. The British Museum says the trip covered thousands of miles.

Vermeil's root word means little worm. Vermeil is sterling silver coated with a thick layer of gold, and sterling silver is at least 92.5 percent pure silver. In the United States the gold must be at least 10 karat. It must also equal about 2.5 microns of pure gold, which is thicker than the minimum for gold plate. The word is French for bright red, and its root is Latin for little worm, the insect behind red dye. Old gilders ground gold into mercury to make a paste. Heat drove off the mercury and left a gold skin. Today the gold is applied by electroplating.

Tahitian black pearls are not truly black. They grow in the black-lipped pearl oyster of French Polynesia, and colors run from charcoal gray and silver to green and brown. Peacock often means green with a pink overtone. Most are about 9 to 13 millimeters across, and the oyster needs about 18 to 24 months to grow each pearl. Legend says the god Oro brought a black pearl down a rainbow. In the early 1960s, a vet had technicians graft about 5,000 oysters, and the first commercial farm opened on Manihi atoll in 1966. Dealers began selling them on world markets in the early 1970s.

Gems were polished smooth before faceting. A cabochon has a smooth domed top and a flat back. Until the late Middle Ages, gems were simply cut this way, and the V&A says most medieval ring gems are cabochons. Faceting began to spread around the 1400s. Early diamond cuts just polished the crystal's natural faces. A diamond dust wheel, the scaif, arrived in the late 1400s. Star sapphires and cat's-eyes are still cut this way, because facets would hide the star or the eye. Turquoise is most often cut into cabochons.

This ruby was grown in a flame. At 17, French chemist Auguste Verneuil became Edmond Frémy's assistant. He lodged sealed notes in 1891, then announced the method in 1902. Powder falls through an oxygen and hydrogen flame, about 2,000 degrees Celsius. The powder melts and builds up as a crystal called a boule. A little chromium mixed into the powder makes it red. It is corundum, the same mineral as natural ruby, and curved growth lines and gas bubbles help gemologists spot it. Flame fusion is still a common way to make synthetic ruby, and tiny synthetic rubies also serve as bearings inside watches.

This opal turns clear in water. It is a hydrophane opal, which soaks up water like a sponge. Much of the opal from Ethiopia's Welo Province is hydrophane, and the main find came in 2008, near the town of Wegel Tena. A soaked stone can gain up to 15 percent in weight, and drying back to its usual look can take days. Its play of color is often vivid, like Australian opal, but Ethiopian opal formed in volcanic rock, unlike Australia's sedimentary opal. This garnet has more fire than diamond. Demantoid is the green variety of andradite garnet, and the name comes from an old German word for diamond. Its fire, called dispersion, measures 0.057, against 0.044 for diamond. Chromium makes it green, and iron can push it toward yellow. Turn this gem and its color changes. It is iolite, the gem variety of the mineral cordierite, and the name comes from a Greek word for violet. Damascene jewelry is gold hammered into steel. Damascene work inlays gold or silver wire into iron or steel. Its name alludes to Damascus, the Syrian city. First the steel is scored with a fine crosshatch pattern. Then the wire is hammered into the scored surface. Last, the steel is blackened in a hot bath, called pavonado. In Toledo, Spain, workshops still make it by hand. In 1761 King Charles III founded a royal arms factory in Toledo. The Zuloaga family revived the craft in Eibar in the 1860s. In January 2026 Toledo's damascene craft became a protected cultural asset.

The phrase acid test began with gold. Dictionaries say it comes from testing gold with nitric acid. On base metal the acid fizzes and turns green or gray, but pure gold is a noble metal and nitric acid cannot dissolve it. A mix of two acids called aqua regia does dissolve gold. Jewelers still use acid kits to check the karat of gold. The touchstone method is at least 2,500 years old, and touchstones were once called Lydian stones, for Lydia's gold. The Greek word for touchstone, basanos, also meant a test. By 1854, acid test meant any decisive test.

Palladium is named for an asteroid. Heinrich Olbers found the asteroid Pallas in March 1802. The asteroid is named for the goddess Pallas Athena. Around 1802 the chemist William Wollaston named his new metal after it. In 1803 he sold it anonymously as Palladium, or New Silver. A rival chemist called it an alloy of platinum and mercury. Wollaston offered 20 pounds to anyone who could make it. Nobody did. It is naturally white and the lightest metal in the platinum group. Jewelers began using it around 1939, when platinum was needed for war. A 950 stamp means the piece is 95 percent palladium.

Gold is not weighed in regular ounces. A troy ounce is 31.1 grams, against 28.35 grams for an everyday ounce. A troy pound has just 12 ounces, so it is the lighter pound. Many jewelers use pennyweights, and 20 of them make a troy ounce. A pennyweight is 24 grains, or about 1.55 grams. The system is usually thought to be named for Troyes, France. In 1527, England made troy weight official for gold and silver, and it is still the standard for gold and other precious metals today. Karat measures purity in 24ths, so 18 karat is 75 percent gold.

Liberty's copper skin is hammered like jewelry. The Statue of Liberty's skin is hand hammered copper. The method is called repoussé, hammering the metal from behind. Jewelers do the same with a hammer and punch on sheet gold. Sculptor Bartholdi designed it, and work began in France in 1875. Workers hammered the sheets over wooden forms. The copper is only 2.4 millimeters thick, about two pennies. More than 300 separate sheets make up the skin. Gustave Eiffel designed the iron framework that holds it up. Cloisonné color is powdered glass. The name comes from French cloisons, meaning partitions. Thin wire is soldered onto a metal base to make cells. Each cell is filled with glass enamel, as powder or paste. Then the piece is fired until the glass melts. The glass shrinks, so the cells are refilled and fired again. Last, it is ground and polished until the wire edges show. Six gold rings from a Cyprus tomb are over 3,000 years old. Its great age was Byzantine, from the 10th to the 12th century. Makers used it almost only on gold, often for tiny saints.

A meteorite impact made this green gem. Moldavite is a natural glass, not a crystal. The Ries impact in southern Germany happened about 15 million years ago, and the blast melted rock that cooled into green glass. Rhinestones are named for the Rhine River. It translates the French caillou du Rhin, meaning Rhine pebble. The first ones were said to be rock crystal from the Rhine. Clear rock crystal was a cheap way to imitate diamond. Today rhinestones are usually glass or paste. Georg Friedrich Strass, an Alsatian jeweler, worked in Paris around 1730. He coated the underside of lead glass with metal powder. Strass still means rhinestone in many European languages. Daniel Swarovski patented an electric machine for cutting crystal in 1892. He founded his firm in Wattens, Austria, in 1895.

Shakespeare's will left money to buy rings. The will is dated 25 March 1616 and has three pages, and three of his six known signatures are on its pages. Three fellow actors each got 26 shillings and 8 pence for rings, and two more friends were left the same sum for a ring each. The actors' ring money was squeezed in between the lines, and one friend named for a ring was crossed out and replaced. Leaving money for memorial rings was a common custom for centuries. A gold ring marked WS found in 1810 is still debated. The original will is kept at The National Archives in Kew.

A hole in a ring tells time. It is called a ring dial, a small brass sundial, and many hung from a thumb or from a neck cord. Sunlight passes through a tiny pinhole in the ring, and a dot of light lands on an hour scale inside the ring. The light itself shows the hour, with no shadow. You slide the pinhole to the month first. Some rings are engraved with the latitudes where they work best. Shakespeare may mention one in As You Like It, from 1599. Museums in London and Basel hold ring dials from the 1700s.

The crown weighs nearly five pounds, and its hundreds of stones include amethysts and topazes. George V had the stones set permanently in 1911. It is used only for the moment of crowning. After that, the monarch switches to the Imperial State Crown, which is only about half as heavy. Charles III was crowned with it in 2023, and before then its band was adjusted to fit King Charles.

Ghana's money is named after a seashell. The cedi comes from an Akan word for cowrie shell. Cowries were used as money in Asia and Africa for centuries, and a Chinese queen's tomb from the Shang dynasty held about 7,000 cowries. The Chinese character for cowrie sits inside many words about money, and China later cast bronze copies of cowrie shells. In AD 9, Wang Mang even tried to bring shell money back. Many traded cowries came from the Maldives, in the Indian Ocean. The same shells also made jewelry and hair ornaments, and in parts of Africa, cowries were used as money into the 1800s.

Frying a mussel ruined a giant pearl. In 1857, a man in New Jersey fried mussels from Notch Brook, and he bit into a pearl that weighed about 100 carats. The frying had destroyed its shine. Soon after, another man found a pink pearl in the same brook. It weighed 93 grains, and by most accounts Tiffany paid $1,500. It reached Empress Eugenie of France and became the Queen Pearl. People rushed in, and within months the brook had no mussels left. The craze spread to streams in other states over the next decades. In the 1890s, Tiffany's gem expert studied American pearls.

Men's wedding rings were once considered odd. Fortune magazine said so in 1947, in a piece called Ring Twice. Men mostly wore signet and graduation rings instead, and in 1926 an ad campaign for men's engagement rings flopped. Many soldiers wore wedding rings in World War II to remember home, and a 1944 ad showed a soldier with a ring reading a letter. The jewelry industry promoted double ring weddings on radio and in schools. Jewelers called the idea the double ring service. Fortune counted double ring weddings rising from 15 to 80 percent. By the early 1950s a groom's ring was standard.

Pliny said one knot heals wounds faster. It is called the Hercules knot, or the Herakles knot, and Greek goldsmiths tied it into gold diadems and bracelets. It was popular in jewelry by the 300s BCE, and a British Museum diadem with this knot is over 2,300 years old. Legend says Hercules knotted the paws of his lion skin. This jewel says who ordered it made. The Alfred Jewel has an Old English inscription around its edge that reads, Alfred ordered me to be made. Gold frames a tiny enamel figure under a cover of rock crystal, and the green-robed figure may stand for the sense of sight. It was reportedly plowed up in a field in Somerset in 1693. Its base is a dragon-like head with a socket for a rod, so it may have topped an aestel, a pointer for following the words in a book. In the preface to his Pastoral Care, Alfred wrote that each copy would carry an aestel worth fifty mancuses, and a mancus was worth roughly a month's wages. Today the jewel is on display in the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford.

Marcasite jewelry contains no marcasite. The sparkly stones are really pyrite, also called fool's gold. Both minerals are iron sulfide with the same formula, but their atoms are arranged differently, so their crystals differ. Real marcasite can crumble into powder in humid air, and museums keep real marcasite in dry rooms. Jewelers cut tiny faceted pieces of pyrite and set them in silver. Pyrite's name means fire, since it makes sparks against steel, and wheellock guns used pyrite to make sparks. In Georgian times, pyrite pieces stood in for diamonds. Pre-Columbian artists made mirrors from cut pyrite pieces.

The phrase first water began with diamonds. In the gem trade, water meant a stone's clearness, and a perfect diamond was the clearest drop of water. There were three ranks, from first water down to third. Some think it came from Arabic, where water also means luster. Shakespeare wrote of diamonds of a most praised water around 1607. By about 1800 people used it for anything the very best, and it even described crooks, like a swindler of the first water. Jewelers once called the most colorless diamonds river or first water. GIA's D to Z color scale arrived in 1953.

Gold-filled jewelry needs only five percent gold. In the United States, that means at least one twentieth of the total weight, in a layer of ten karat gold or better that covers every surface and is bonded to a base metal core by mechanical means. The layer is much thicker than regular plating, so it lasts longer. Gold electroplate needs only 0.175 microns of gold. Vermeil has a sterling silver base under its gold, and its gold layer must be at least ten karat and 2.5 microns thick. Rolled gold plate has half as much gold as gold-filled, which is one fortieth of the total weight.

The word crystal once meant ice. In Greek the word krystallos first meant plain ice, and later it also named clear quartz, which is rock crystal. Many ancient writers believed rock crystal was ice frozen for good. The Roman writer Pliny said crystal is a kind of ice and wrote that it forms where winter snow freezes hardest. He said it cannot bear heat, so it suits cold drinks. Rock crystal is clear quartz, which is silicon dioxide. Greek jewelers set it in bracelets and carved it into seals. English has used the word crystal since before the 12th century.

This emerald has a wheel inside. A trapiche emerald shows a pattern like a wheel with six spokes, and it is very rare. The dark arms are mostly carbon, and green emerald fills the gaps between them. The name is Spanish, after the cogwheels used in sugar mills. Almost all come from a few mines in western Colombia, such as Muzo, and a very few have turned up in Brazil and Madagascar. Cutters often polish them into smooth domes called cabochons to show off the six sections. The pattern stays fixed when you tilt the stone, unlike a star effect. Scientists still do not agree on how it forms.

Venice banned its glassmakers from leaving. Around 1291, Venice moved its glass furnaces to the island of Murano, and the reason given was the risk of fire. Glassmakers were forbidden to leave or to teach their secrets to outsiders, but many left anyway, despite heavy penalties. Venetian glass beads are documented from the early 1300s. Lampwork beads are shaped by melting glass rods over a flame, and chevron beads are cut from hollow rods of layered, colored glass. Women then threaded the finished beads onto strings, and merchants shipped them as trade goods to Africa and the Americas. UNESCO listed glass bead making as cultural heritage in 2020.

The oldest known geological map shows gold. It was drawn in Egypt around 1150 BC, under Ramesses IV, and it shows Wadi Hammamat, between the Nile and the Red Sea. The mapped stretch is about 9 miles long. It marks gold deposits and four small houses for the workers, and pink hills mark granite and gold-bearing quartz. A caption says the gold mountains are colored red. It was prepared for an expedition to quarry stone for royal statues, and south sits at the top of the map. It is kept in the Museo Egizio in Turin, Italy. The next known geological map came nearly 3,000 years later.

Only one gem can be called cat's-eye. In the trade, plain cat's-eye means the gem chrysoberyl, and other stones need a prefix, like quartz cat's-eye. A band of light reflects from thin, parallel inclusions inside the stone, and the stone is cut as a cabochon so the band shows. The cutter lines the base up with those inclusions. Jewelers call the light and dark halves milk and honey. Its colors run from honey brown to greenish yellow, and it measures 8.5 on the Mohs scale. Sri Lanka and Brazil are two main sources. Alexandrite is a color-change variety of the same mineral.

This pink gem is Argentina's national stone. The name rhodochrosite comes from Greek words meaning rose color, and it is made of manganese carbonate, which is rose red when pure. Calcium or magnesium in the mix lightens it to pink. Argentina named it the national gemstone in 2002, and the banded Inca rose comes from the Capillitas mine in Catamarca. That banded material is usually cut into cabochons or beads. It is soft, about 3.5 to 4 on the Mohs scale, and it has perfect cleavage, so it needs gentle care. Colorado's Sweet Home Mine produced the Alma King crystal in 1992. In 2002, Colorado also named it the state mineral.

Some diamonds glow blue under UV light. Roughly 25 to 35 percent of gem diamonds fluoresce to some degree, and more than 95 percent of those glow blue under UV light. A gap surrounded by three nitrogen atoms usually causes the blue glow. In 1663, Robert Boyle reported a diamond that shone in the dark, and George Stokes coined the word fluorescence in 1852. He took the name from fluorspar, a mineral that also glows. GIA reports it from none to very strong. Daylight includes long-wave UV, the light that sets off the blue glow. In daylight, blue fluorescence can make a yellowish diamond look whiter.

Miners reportedly used diamonds as game tokens. The story comes from Brazil in the 1720s. Until then, India was the world's main source of diamonds. Gold miners there found shiny stones in rivers and streams, and later accounts say some used them as markers in card games. Then someone who had been in India recognized them. Then in the 1860s, diamonds turned up in South Africa.

This pink pearl comes from a snail. It comes from the queen conch, a large Caribbean sea snail, and unlike an oyster pearl, a conch pearl has no nacre. Its surface has a shimmering pattern called flame structure, and parallel fibers of aragonite crystal create that silky shimmer. Collectors prize pink stones, especially a salmon pink. Reportedly, about one conch in 10,000 makes a pearl. Conch pearls were popular in Victorian jewelry, then revived in the 1980s. In 2024, the United States listed the queen conch as threatened. In 2009, researchers developed a technique to seed conch pearls.

This purple gem comes from one place. Charoite is known from only one place, in Russia's Sakha Republic, and geologists reportedly found it in the 1940s. It was officially recognized as a mineral in the late 1970s. Its swirls come from fibrous crystals growing in interlocking patterns, and its colors range from lilac to violet. It measures 5 to 6 on the Mohs scale and is usually carved or cut into cabochons. Mining is said to be limited to about 100 tons a year, and some pieces also show a cat's-eye glow called chatoyancy. The gem is named for the Chara River, about 43 miles away.

Cubic zirconia came from a laser lab. Scientists at the Lebedev Physical Institute in Moscow developed it while looking for a crystal to use in lasers, and the team published its growing method in 1973. In Russia, it is called fianit, after the institute's abbreviation, FIAN. Radio waves melt the zirconia inside a water-cooled container, and a solid crust called the skull forms around the melt. Zirconia melts at about 2,700 degrees Celsius. Colorless stones reached the jewelry market in 1976. It rates about 8 on the Mohs scale, and diamond rates 10. A CZ weighs about 1.7 times as much as a same-size diamond.

Some Herkimer diamonds hold hardened petroleum. Herkimer diamonds are really clear quartz crystals, and each crystal has a point at both ends. A wedding gift began sweetheart brooches. On their wedding day in 1886, the Earl of Airlie gave his wife a brooch copying his regiment's badge, and she said other army wives copied her. They spread in the Boer War and boomed in World War One. They were small copies of regimental cap badges, and hundreds of designs were made, mostly in London and Birmingham. Soldiers bought them at jewelry shops and army camps. Despite the name, they also went to mothers and sisters, and women wore them with pride and as good luck charms. Museums from London to Canberra hold them today.

This jewelry enamel has no metal backing. It is called plique-à-jour, which means open to light. Thin wires form tiny cells on a temporary backing, and clear enamel is fused into the cells. Then the backing is removed, sometimes by dissolving it in acid. The result looks like a tiny stained glass window, and light can shine straight through the finished enamel. French jewelers rediscovered it in the 1860s. René Lalique used it in jewelry around the year 1900, and Norwegian firms showed it at the 1900 Paris exhibition. A single piece can take up to four months.

A goldsmith built Florence's giant dome. Filippo Brunelleschi trained as a goldsmith as a teenager, and around 1400 he made small silver figures for an altar. In 1401 seven artists competed to make the Baptistery doors. The two finalists were both trained goldsmiths, and Lorenzo Ghiberti won the commission. In 1420 work began on his dome for Florence Cathedral, and it was finished in 1436, apart from the lantern. Over four million bricks went into it. Many sources call it the largest masonry dome ever built. His hoist ran on oxen and could reverse without turning them.

This amber can turn blue in sunlight. Most blue amber is mined in the Dominican Republic, in the north near the city of Santiago. Its age is debated, but 15 to 20 million years is common. The blue is fluorescence, set off by the ultraviolet light in sunlight, and it shows best against a dark background. Hold it up to the light and it looks plain yellow, because the blue sits on the surface of the stone. A hydrocarbon called perylene is the likely cause, and blue amber costs more than ordinary amber. Amber floats in salt water, which helps expose glass fakes.

Bahrain bans the sale of cultured pearls. Bahrain was the center of the Gulf pearl trade, and divers went out for about four months each summer. They wore a nose clip and leather caps on their fingers, and a stone weight on a rope pulled them down to the oysters. The merchants who bought the pearls were called tawash. In the 1930s, cultured pearls from Japan helped end the old trade. In 2012, UNESCO listed Bahrain's pearling path as a World Heritage site, and Bahrain's DANAT lab tells natural pearls from cultured ones. Today, cultured pearls are barred from its jewelry counters.

The diamond anniversary is the 60th. Silver marks the 25th year and gold marks the 50th, and some lists also give diamond to the 75th. Silver and gold anniversaries are traced to German-speaking lands, where couples were given a silver wreath, then later a gold one. In 1937, an American jewelers' association introduced an expanded list. Pearl is for the 30th and ruby for the 40th. Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee in 1897 marked 60 years on the throne, and platinum marks the 70th year in the British list. The Queen and Prince Philip marked a platinum anniversary in 2017.

Emerald has a rare red cousin. Red beryl is a rare color of beryl, the emerald mineral, and trace manganese gives it a raspberry red color. Maynard Bixby found it in Utah's Thomas Range in 1904, and the name bixbite was dropped to avoid confusion with bixbyite. Utah's Wah Wah Mountains are the only known commercial source. Reportedly, one red beryl crystal is found per 150,000 diamonds, and most cut stones weigh well under one carat. It is hard, at 7.5 to 8 on the Mohs scale, and the color forms as the crystal grows, not from treatment. It is sometimes called red emerald.

This 2,000-year-old crown folds for travel. In 1978, a Soviet-Afghan team led by Viktor Sarianidi found it. It came from six graves, for five women and one man, and they held more than 20,000 items of gold and precious metal. The treasures were later hidden in Kabul's presidential palace vault, and only a handful of trusted people knew. In 2004, the keys to the gold safe could not be found, so a locksmith opened it with a circular saw. About 30 people watched, including the archaeologist who found it. It then toured museums from Paris to New York.

This gem is fossilized wood. Whitby jet formed about 180 million years ago, in the Jurassic, and some say the trees were relatives of the monkey puzzle. The best known source is the coast near Whitby, England. Jet is light and feels warm to the touch, it is soft yet takes a high polish, and rubbed with wool it can build up an electric charge. Jet has been found in Bronze Age burial sites in Britain. Queen Victoria wore it in mourning after Prince Albert died in 1861, and by the early 1870s about 1,500 people worked in Whitby's jet trade. Imitation jet was often black glass, sometimes called French jet.

This opal was once a seashell. Opalized shells have been found at Lightning Ridge, Australia. Opal can fill the space left when a fossil dissolves, and Australia's opal fossils are about 100 million years old, from when a shallow inland sea covered central Australia. Silica rich water filled the voids where shells and bones lay, and tiny silica spheres in opal break light into rainbow colors. At Lightning Ridge, opal has even replaced a dinosaur's jaw, and pinecones have turned to opal there too. A miner found Eric, an opalized sea reptile, in 1987, and public donations of over $500,000 helped buy Eric.

Pearl necklaces are full of tiny knots. Most pearl necklaces have a knot between each pearl, so if the strand breaks, usually only one pearl comes loose, and the knots also keep pearls from rubbing against each other. Pearls are often strung on silk, but silk stretches and weakens, so a strand worn often may need restringing about once a year. Stringers tie each knot by hand with fine tweezers or an awl, and French wire, also called bullion, often protects the thread at the clasp. Pearls are drilled, and the cord is sized to the hole. A princess length strand is about 17 to 19 inches.

Flawless means no flaws at 10x. The Gemological Institute of America's clarity scale has 11 grades. Features inside a diamond are called inclusions, and blemishes are only on the surface, such as scratches or nicks. Flawless means neither is visible under 10x magnification. The institute introduced its 10x loupe in 1934, the final grade is always set under that loupe, and the institute built its grading system in the early 1950s. Graders weigh how big each feature is and where it sits. Flawless is rare, because few diamonds are free of inclusions, and most slightly included diamonds show no inclusions visible to the naked eye.

Platinum is white without any plating. White gold is an alloy, usually coated in rhodium that wears off, while platinum is naturally white and needs no coating. Jewelry platinum is usually about 95 percent pure, stamped 950, and jewelers like it for prongs because it is strong and wears slowly. It is denser than gold, so a platinum ring feels heavier, and when it scratches the metal mostly gets pushed aside, leaving a soft patina a jeweler can polish bright. Diamond moves heat better than silver. It carries heat about five times better than copper or silver, as vibrations in tightly bonded carbon atoms, yet most diamonds block electricity, the opposite of a metal. Jewelers use that to test stones with a heated metal probe, because a diamond pulls heat from the tip fast and the tip cools. Cubic zirconia and glass pull heat away slowly, so they read differently. Moissanite can pass a thermal test like diamond, but under magnification it shows doubled facet edges. Thermal testers for jewelers date from the late 1970s, and today diamond layers also help spread heat in power chips.

Only a diamond can polish a diamond. Diamond is the hardest natural material, ranking 10 on the Mohs scale, so polishers grind with dust made from other diamonds. The dust is mixed with olive oil and goes onto a spinning cast iron wheel called a scaife. Cutters must work with the grain, because some directions barely polish. To shape a stone's outline, two diamonds are rubbed together, and the dust that rubs off is collected and put to use. Tradition credits Lodewyk van Bercken of Bruges with the scaife in 1476, though some historians doubt it. A round brilliant has 57 or 58 facets, depending on the culet.

The first laser used a ruby rod. Theodore Maiman built it at Hughes Research Laboratories in Malibu, and it first fired on May 16, 1960. The rod was a small piece of pink synthetic ruby, about the size of a fingertip. Ruby is aluminum oxide with a little chromium in it, and a flash lamp excited the chromium atoms, which gave off red light with a wavelength of about 694 nanometers. A leading physics journal turned down his paper, and Nature published it in August 1960 instead. Seven months later, Bell Labs built the first gas laser.

Most rainbow moonstone is a different mineral. Moonstone is a feldspar with thin alternating layers inside, and light scatters off those layers in a glow called adularescence. That word comes from the Adula mountains in the Swiss Alps. A smooth dome cut, called a cabochon, shows the glow best, and the most prized stones are colorless with a blue sheen. Moonstone is one of the modern June birthstones. Rainbow moonstone is usually labradorite, a different feldspar.

Sterling silver is only 92.5 percent silver. The other 7.5 percent is usually copper, because pure silver is too soft, and copper adds strength. A 925 stamp means 925 parts silver per thousand. In 1697 England added a purer standard, called Britannia silver, which aimed to stop people melting coins for silverware. Silver tarnishes when sulfur gases in the air react with it, and polishing removes a little silver each time. The word sterling may come from a coin stamped with a star. Until 1920, British silver coins were sterling silver.

The best diamond color grade is D. The Gemological Institute of America introduced this scale in 1953, and its president, Richard Liddicoat, was the architect of the system. Older systems used letters like triple A and phrases like blue white, and the institute wanted a fresh start, with no link to older grades. So it began at D, a letter not tied to top quality. The scale has 23 letters, running from D to Z, and D to F are colorless while G to J are near colorless. Graders compare each diamond with master stones, table down, in controlled light. The D to Z scale measures how little color a diamond has.

Napoleon's sword once held this diamond. The Regent is named for a regent of France who once owned it. It was reportedly found at Golconda, India, around 1698, and the rough stone weighed more than 400 carats. Thomas Pitt, governor of Madras, bought it around 1701, and cutting it in London took about two years. The finished cushion cut stone weighs about 140 carats. In 1717 Pitt sold it to Philippe, Duke of Orléans. In 1722 it was set in Louis XV's coronation crown, and it sat on Napoleon's sword at his 1804 coronation. The Regent has been in the Louvre's collection since 1887.

Sunlight can fade this pink gem. Kunzite can fade when exposed to heat and bright light. It was found near Pala, California, in 1902, and chemist Charles Baskerville named it after George Kunz of Tiffany. Kunzite is the pink to lilac variety of the mineral spodumene, and trace amounts of manganese give it that color. Its color changes with the viewing direction, an effect called pleochroism, so cutters usually orient it to show the deepest pink through the top. Its hardness is 6.5 to 7, with two perfect cleavage directions. Brazil and Afghanistan are two of its main sources, and the Smithsonian holds an 880 carat heart-shaped kunzite from Brazil.

A prince sent her a painted eye. In 1785, the Prince of Wales wrote to Maria Fitzherbert, and with his letter came a tiny eye painted by Richard Cosway. About a thousand are known to survive, and the biggest known collection, in Alabama, holds about a hundred.

Vikings paid with jewelry cut by weight. Silver was paid by weight, so merchants carried small scales, and much of that silver arrived as Islamic coins from the east. Arm rings turned silver into wealth a person could wear, and when payment was due, a ring could be cut into pieces. Those pieces are known today as hack silver. Lords also gave arm rings to followers as rewards, and the Old English poem Beowulf calls a king a giver of rings. Old Norse poets said ring-breaker for a generous leader. Merchants' small weights still turn up at Viking sites.

This quartz is two gems in one. Ametrine is a quartz crystal with purple and gold zones, and its name combines amethyst and citrine. Iron in the crystal gives each zone its color, and cut stones often show an even split between the two colors. It has a hardness of seven on the Mohs scale, and commercial natural ametrine comes only from Bolivia's Anahí mine. Legend says a Spanish conquistador got the mine as a princess's dowry, and he reportedly gave its stones to the Spanish crown. The mine was rediscovered in the 1960s, and ametrine returned to the market in the 1970s.

California's state gem was mistaken for sapphire. Blue crystals turned up in California's San Benito County, and a prospector reportedly thought they were sapphire. Berkeley's George Louderback identified it as a new mineral in 1907 and named it benitoite, after the San Benito region. Most benitoite is violetish blue, and pink stones are very rare. This square diamond has its corners cut. Joseph Asscher of Amsterdam developed the Asscher cut in 1902, and its square outline has cropped corners that read as an octagon. The original design has 58 facets, and a high crown and deep pavilion create a hall of mirrors effect. It became popular in the 1920s, during the Art Deco era, and production of the original stopped around World War II. Asscher's firm also cut the Cullinan diamond in Amsterdam in 1908, and in 1980 Queen Juliana granted the firm the title Royal. Around 2001 the family introduced the Royal Asscher cut with 74 facets. An Asscher cut is square, while an emerald cut is rectangular.

Cleopatra's emerald mines probably weren't hers. They are in Egypt's Eastern Desert, inland from the Red Sea, and the Romans called the area Mons Smaragdus, or Emerald Mountain. Miners reportedly worked there for some 2,000 years, and then the mines were forgotten outside Egypt for centuries. Frédéric Cailliaud, trained as a jeweler, rediscovered them around 1816. Egyptian emeralds were often paler and cloudier than Colombian ones, and Egypt led until Colombian emeralds reached Europe in the 1500s. Legend links Cleopatra to emeralds, but the mines' nickname probably came from Victorian jewelers' marketing. Emerald is a green beryl, colored mainly by chromium.

Diamonds and pencil lead share one element. Both are pure carbon, and only the arrangement of the atoms differs. In diamond, each atom bonds to four others in a rigid lattice. In graphite, each atom bonds to three others in flat sheets, and those sheets slip past each other, so graphite is soft. Pencil lead has no lead in it because graphite was once mistaken for lead. Diamond is 10 on the Mohs scale and graphite is about 1 to 2. Natural diamonds form deep underground, more than 100 kilometers down, and some labs grow diamonds from graphite using high pressure and heat. A diamond conducts heat very well, and heated enough in oxygen it burns and becomes carbon dioxide.

A ring once served as a signature. A signet ring has a design carved into its face, and pressed into soft wax it leaves a raised print, or seal. The design is carved in reverse so the print reads correctly. Mesopotamians rolled cylinder seals on clay over 5,000 years ago, Egyptians used scarab seals about 4,000 years ago, and about 2,000 years ago Romans used signet rings to seal letters. In medieval England a seal often stood in for a signature, and deeds were not usually signed until the 1500s. Tough stones like carnelian were popular for seal faces. Each new pope still receives a signet ring called the Fisherman's Ring.

Ruby and sapphire are one mineral. Both are corundum, a mineral made of aluminum and oxygen. A trace of chromium makes ruby red, and iron and titanium color blue sapphire. Corundum in other colors is usually called a sapphire, and where pink becomes ruby depends on who you ask: GIA needs red to dominate, but some groups accept any red corundum. Ruby's name comes from ruber, the Latin word for red, and sapphire comes from a Greek name for a blue stone, probably lapis. Myanmar's Mogok area is one of the most famous ruby sources. Both rank 9 on the Mohs scale, and only diamond is harder.

Gold is yellow largely thanks to relativity. Gold atoms are very heavy, and their inner electrons move at more than half the speed of light. At such speeds Einstein's relativity starts to matter: it squeezes the atom's electron layers and shifts their energy gaps. So gold soaks up blue light, and what bounces back looks yellow. Silver only absorbs invisible ultraviolet light, so it looks like a mirror. Gold is one of very few metals that aren't silvery. Chemists have studied this effect since the 1970s, and calculations suggest the same effect helps keep mercury liquid and that gold would look silvery without relativity.

Named for a daughter and the sea. Larimar is a blue variety of the mineral pectolite, and traces of copper are believed to color its sky blue. It is known only from the Dominican Republic. Father Miguel Domingo Fuertes is credited with finding it in 1916, and then it was forgotten for decades. A Peace Corps volunteer and Miguel Méndez rediscovered it in 1974, and blue pebbles on the coast reportedly led searchers upriver to the source. Much of it is dug by hand in narrow shafts and tunnels. Méndez combined his daughter Larissa's name with mar, Spanish for sea. Larimar is soft, so keep it away from heat and harsh chemicals.

This metal looks like wood grain. It is called mokume-gane, which means wood-grain metal, and swirling layers of differently colored metals make the pattern. Metalworkers in Japan developed it in the 1600s for sword fittings, and Denbei Shoami is usually credited with it. Makers stack thin metal sheets, then fuse them with heat and pressure, and typical layers are copper and silver, sometimes with gold. The block is carved or drilled to expose the layers, then hammered flat so the wood-grain pattern appears. Because each piece is hand-made, no two match exactly. Tiffany reportedly showed mokume silver at the 1889 Paris world's fair, and centuries later jewelers took it up for rings.

A squid's cousin became a gemstone. Ammolite comes from the fossil shells of ammonites, extinct sea animals that were distant cousins of squid and octopus. They lived about 70 to 75 million years ago, and gem-quality ammolite is mined commercially only in southern Alberta. Stacked layers of aragonite bend light into rainbow colors, and red and green are the most common while blue is rare. Jewelers usually back the thin layer with shale and cap it with clear quartz. The Blackfoot call fossil ammonite stones iniskim, or buffalo stones, and in one story a singing stone called the buffalo back. In 2022, Alberta made ammolite its official gemstone.

Most diamonds are older than dinosaurs. Many natural diamonds are one to three billion years old, while the first dinosaurs appeared about 245 million years ago. Diamonds form more than 90 miles down in Earth's mantle, where the pressure is crushing and the heat is around 1,000 degrees Celsius, and a rare volcanic eruption can carry them to the surface. The oldest diamonds dated so far came from northern Canada and are about 3.5 billion years old, and Earth itself is about 4.5 billion years old.

A jeweler's box hid a new mineral. In 1945, Dublin gemologist Richard Taaffe bought a box of old stones, sorted them by color and checked each under a microscope. One mauve stone looked like spinel, which bends light one way, but this stone bent light two ways. London lab tests confirmed a new mineral, named taaffeite in 1951, and it is the first mineral identified from a cut gem. Its colors range from lilac and violet to pink and red, and it comes mostly from Sri Lanka, with a few finds in Tanzania. Early stones now sit in London's Natural History Museum, and even now it ranks among the rarest gemstones.

What pavé means and how it's set

Pavé is French for paved: small stones set close together so the metal looks paved. Each stone is often a hundredth of a carat, held by small beads of metal that a setter raises with a graver, and micro pavé goes down to half a millimeter. The renders in this video were made from the ring's 3D file with HeyGema.

#pave #diamondring #jewelrymaking #stonesetting #cadjewelry

How a 3D file becomes a gold ring

Lost-wax casting, from the 3D file to the finished ring. The file is printed in a castable resin, set on a wax tree, covered in plaster and baked at about 730°C until the resin burns out. Gold goes into the space it left, and the mold is broken to get the ring out, so each mold is used once. The renders in this video were made from the ring's 3D file with HeyGema.

#jewelrymaking #lostwaxcasting #jewelrycasting #3dprinting #cadjewelry

Why rose gold is pink

Rose gold is pink because of copper. 18 karat gold is 75% gold, and the other metals set the color. Most jewelers lose clients not because of their work but because of how they present it.

1. You still email PDFs of your designs
